_readme: SAIRNlaw deadline engine seed -- Pennsylvania civil litigation. Phase 3,
state jurisdiction #4 of 4 (OH/IN/MI/PA). The last of the set.
Every value below was read from primary source on 2026-08-22 and is quoted
in the row. Nothing was carried over from Ohio, Indiana or Michigan. By
this point three states in the set already disagreed with each other on the
short-period question alone, so there was no pattern left to generalise
from even if that had been acceptable.
FINDING 1 -- THE RULE-NUMBER CONFLICT IS RESOLVED, AND BOTH SOURCES WERE
RIGHT AT DIFFERENT TIMES. The question going in was whether Pa.R.C.P. 106
or 201 Pa. Code Sec. 107 governs civil-deadline computation. Answer, from
the Pennsylvania Bulletin and the Pennsylvania Code directly:
* Pa.R.C.P. 106 (231 Pa. Code Sec. 106) is RESCINDED. The Bulletin prints
it as 'Rule 106. [Computation of Time] [Rescinded].', effective
* Pa.R.J.A. 107 (201 Pa. Code Sec. 107) is the CURRENT governing rule,
'Added November 3, 2023, effective January 1, 2024.'
* The adoption report states the new rule 'is a consolidation of
Pa.R.Civ.P. 106-108 and reflects the Court's prior use of 1 Pa.C.S.
Sec. 1908 for the computation of time.'
So this was not one source being wrong -- it was a rule set that moved
between two titles on 2024-01-01, and a search that surfaced both eras at
once. Anything relying on Pa.R.C.P. 106 today is citing a rescinded rule.
CONSEQUENCE, AND THE FIRST REAL USE OF THE ENGINE'S EFFECTIVE-WINDOW
FEATURE: the rules below carry effective_from 2024-01-01, the date the
current computation standard took effect. A Pennsylvania matter triggered
BEFORE that date is REFUSED with NO_RULE_IN_FORCE rather than computed.
That is deliberate. The pre-2024 Pa.R.C.P. 106 text was never read verbatim
in this pass, and encoding a rule from a paraphrase is exactly the guess
this engine refuses to make. The refusal names the window so a caller can
see why. Note the 20-day count in Pa.R.C.P. 1026 itself is much older than
2024 and was NOT rescinded -- what changed on 2024-01-01 is the computation
standard it is paired with, and a rule row here is that pairing.
FINDING 2 -- NO SHORT-PERIOD EXCLUSION. Pa.R.J.A. 107 was read in full,
all four subdivisions: (a) days, (b) omitted days, (c) successive weeks,
(d) months. There is no exclusion of intermediate Saturdays, Sundays or
holidays for short periods anywhere in it. Pennsylvania counts straight
through and omits only the last day, like Michigan and modern FRCP, unlike
Ohio and Indiana. Final tally across this phase: two states have a
seven-day exclusion, two have none. Generalising from either pair would
have been wrong half the time.
FINDING 3 -- PENNSYLVANIA COUNTS TWO SOVEREIGNS' HOLIDAYS, WHICH NO OTHER
JURISDICTION IN THIS SYSTEM DOES. Pa.R.J.A. 107(b), quoted verbatim:
'Whenever the last day of any such period shall fall on Saturday or Sunday,
or on any day made a legal holiday by the laws of this Commonwealth OR OF
THE UNITED STATES, such day shall be omitted from the computation.' The
operative set is therefore the UNION of 44 P.S. Sec. 11 and the federal
list, not either one alone. Practical effect, both directions:
* PA supplies GOOD FRIDAY, FLAG DAY (June 14) and ELECTION DAY, none of
which are federal holidays. Flag Day appears in no other calendar in
this system.
* The UNITED STATES supplies JUNETEENTH, which is absent from 44 P.S.
Sec. 11's own enumeration -- so it counts in Pennsylvania through the
federal limb of 107(b), not through state law. Indiana, whose statute
also omits Juneteenth, has no such federal limb and therefore does NOT
get it. Same missing state statute, opposite outcome, because the
computation rules differ. This is the clearest case in the whole phase
against reasoning from one state's holiday list to another's.
FINDING 4 -- ELECTION DAY IS NARROWER HERE THAN IN INDIANA, AND THAT
MATTERS. Indiana's statute makes a holiday of 'the day of any general,
municipal, or primary election' -- unenumerable statewide. 44 P.S. Sec. 11
names only 'the first Tuesday after the first Monday of November, Election
Day'. That is a single computable date per year, so Pennsylvania's general
election day IS included below (2026-11-03, 2027-11-02, each computed from
the statutory formula). PRIMARY election days are NOT included -- they are
not in the statute, even though Pennsylvania courts in fact close for them
(the state's own 2026 county schedule has a 19-May column). Following the
statute rather than the closure practice is the deliberate call here; see
finding 5 for why that direction is the safe one.
FINDING 5 -- PENNSYLVANIA'S LOCAL VARIANCE IS THE LARGEST IN THE SET, AND
IT PUSHES THE ERROR IN THE DANGEROUS DIRECTION, SO THE ENCODING RULE HAD
TO CHANGE. Michigan authorises local modification in a sentence. The
Pennsylvania courts publish an actual PER-COUNTY MATRIX ('2026 County
Holidays', AOPC, 11/19/2025), which was read directly: sixteen holiday
columns against every county, with counties individually electing to stay
OPEN on particular ones. Bucks County is open on all but one. Chester is
open on Good Friday and Columbus Day. Many counties add closures of their
own (12/24, 12/28, and in one case a county craft day).
Why this changed the approach: for every other limitation disclosed in
this phase, OMITTING a holiday made the computed date EARLIER than the
true one -- the safe direction. Here the risk runs the other way. If a
date is encoded as a holiday but the county in question was open, the
engine rolls a deadline it should not have rolled and reports a date
LATER than the truth, which is how a filing is missed.
So this calendar encodes THE STATUTORY LEGAL TEST -- 44 P.S. Sec. 11 plus
the federal list, which is what Pa.R.J.A. 107(b) actually points to --
and NOT the county closure schedule. Days courts commonly close but no
statute makes a holiday are deliberately EXCLUDED: the day after
Thanksgiving (a column in the state's own matrix), Christmas Eve, primary
election days, and county-specific additions. A Pennsylvania date landing
on or near any of those should be checked against that county's own
schedule before it is relied on.
FINDING 6 -- NO AUTOMATIC MAIL EXTENSION FOUND, AND NONE IS ENCODED.
Pa.R.C.P. 440 governs service of legal papers other than original process
and makes service by mail complete upon mailing; it adds no days. The
additional time referred to by Pa.R.C.P. 1026 is sought under Pa.R.C.P.
248, which is a COURT-GRANTED extension, not an automatic one -- the same
class as Indiana's T.R. 6(B) automatic enlargement, and excluded for the
same reason: it changes the deadline only once someone actually obtains it,
which is a case fact this engine is not given. No service_extension is
attached to any rule below. Unlike the Indiana T.R. 6(G) question, this is
not an unresolved ambiguity -- no automatic three-day mail provision
analogous to FRCP 6(d) was located in the Pennsylvania rules at all.
FINDING 7 -- THE ANSWER PERIOD SPLITS BY SERVICE LOCATION, AS IN MICHIGAN,
BUT ON A DIFFERENT AXIS AND WITH DIFFERENT NUMBERS. Pa.R.C.P. 1026(a): 20
days for a pleading subsequent to the complaint; 60 days for a defendant
served OUTSIDE THE UNITED STATES. Michigan's split was in-state vs.
out-of-state at 21/28; Pennsylvania's is domestic vs. outside the country
at 20/60. Seeded as distinct trigger_events so the engine never guesses,
same treatment as Michigan and as the federal seed's waiver split.
ALSO OBSERVED, NOT ENCODED: Pa.R.C.P. 1026(a)'s twenty-day duty is
conditional -- 'no pleading need be filed unless the preceding pleading
contains a notice to defend or is endorsed with a notice to plead'. Whether
that notice was present is a document fact the engine has no field for. The
condition is quoted in the rule's authority so it appears in the audit
trail an attorney reads, rather than being silently dropped. Pa.R.J.A.
107(c) (successive weeks, with its five-days-between-publications rule) and
107(d) (months, counted excluding the calendar month in which the day
occurs -- a different formulation from this engine's addMonths) are both
unused by any seeded rule and were not built; 107(d) in particular should
NOT be assumed equivalent to the existing months implementation if a
Pennsylvania rule measured in months is ever added.
PHASE 3 IS COMPLETE WITH THIS FILE: OH, IN, MI, PA.

rules.label: Pleading subsequent to the complaint, defendant served within the United States (Pennsylvania)

authority.quote: every pleading subsequent to the complaint shall be filed within twenty days after service of the preceding pleading, but no pleading need be filed unless the preceding pleading contains a notice to defend or is endorsed with a notice to plead
authority.note: THE CONDITION IS PART OF THE RULE: no pleading need be filed at all unless the preceding pleading carried a notice to defend or was endorsed with a notice to plead. Whether it did is a document fact this engine has no field for, so the condition is quoted here to appear in the audit trail rather than silently dropped -- if no such notice was given, this deadline does not run and the date below does not apply. effective_from is 2024-01-01 because that is when Pa.R.J.A. 107 took effect and Pa.R.C.P. 106 was rescinded; the twenty-day count itself is far older and was not rescinded, but this row is the PAIRING of that count with a computation standard, and the pairing is what changed. A matter triggered before 2024-01-01 is refused rather than computed against a rule text never read verbatim -- see _readme finding 1. No service_extension: no automatic mail extension exists in the Pennsylvania rules -- see _readme finding 6.

rules.label: Pleading by a defendant served outside the United States (Pennsylvania)

authority.quote: A defendant served outside the United States shall have sixty days from service of the complaint within which to plead.
authority.note: Distinct trigger_event from the twenty-day rule on purpose -- whether the defendant was served outside the United States is a case fact the engine has no field for and must never guess between two overlapping rules. Note the axis differs from Michigan's: Michigan splits in-state vs. out-of-state (21/28), Pennsylvania splits domestic vs. outside the COUNTRY (20/60). Same effective_from reasoning as the twenty-day rule -- see _readme finding 1.

authority.citation: 44 P.S. Sec. 11 (Pennsylvania legal holidays), together with the federal list, per Pa.R.J.A. 107(b)
authority.note: THE UNION OF TWO SOVEREIGNS' LISTS, because Pa.R.J.A. 107(b) omits a last day falling on a holiday 'by the laws of this Commonwealth or of the United States'. From Pennsylvania: Good Friday (computed 2026-04-03, then confirmed), Flag Day (June 14, unique to this calendar), Columbus Day, and the general Election Day (computed from the statutory formula 'first Tuesday after the first Monday of November' = 2026-11-03). From the United States: Juneteenth, which 44 P.S. Sec. 11 does NOT list -- Pennsylvania gets it through the federal limb, whereas Indiana, whose statute likewise omits it, does not. Independence Day appears twice by design: 2026-07-04 is the statutory date (a Saturday) and 2026-07-03 is the federal observed day under 5 U.S.C. 6103(b); including both is harmless since the statutory date falls on a weekend the engine already excludes. Flag Day 2026 falls on a Sunday, likewise already excluded. DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED, though Pennsylvania courts commonly close: the day after Thanksgiving (2026-11-27, a real column in the AOPC county schedule), Christmas Eve, primary election day (2026-05-19), the Flag Day observed Monday (2026-06-15, which the AOPC itself is marked open for), and all county-specific additions -- none is made a holiday by statute, and encoding a non-holiday would push dates LATER than the truth, the direction that misses a filing. See _readme finding 5.

dates.name: Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. Day
Independence Day (federal observed, July 4 falls on Saturday)

authority.citation: 44 P.S. Sec. 11 (Pennsylvania legal holidays), together with the federal list, per Pa.R.J.A. 107(b)
authority.note: Loaded alongside 2026 so a period triggered late in 2026 does not refuse for a missing year. 2027 is the year Pennsylvania's two-sovereign construction does the most work, each date checked by day-of-week: FLAG DAY falls on a Monday (2027-06-14) and is a real weekday holiday here, something no other calendar in this system can produce at all. Juneteenth falls on a Saturday, so the federal observed Friday 2027-06-18 is included alongside the statutory 2027-06-19. Independence Day falls on a Sunday, so the federal observed Monday 2027-07-05 is included. Christmas Day falls on a Saturday, so the federal observed Friday 2027-12-24 is included alongside the statutory 2027-12-25. Good Friday computed as 2027-03-26 and confirmed. General Election Day computed from the statutory formula as 2027-11-02. Same deliberate exclusions as 2026 -- see _readme finding 5.
